content: Periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, and adenitis (PFAPA) syndrome is a medical condition that typically begins in young children. It is characterized by recurrent episodes of high fever occurring at intervals of approximately 3 to 5 weeks. These febrile episodes are often accompanied by aphthous ulcers, pharyngitis, and/or cervical adenitis. The syndrome was first described in 1987 by Dr. Marshall and was initially named fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, and adenitis (FAPA) syndrome. The name was later changed to PFAPA syndrome to emphasize its periodic nature, which is a hallmark feature of the disorder. There is no established classification system for PFAPA syndrome. The exact pathophysiology of PFAPA remains unclear. However, dysregulation of the innate immune response and inappropriate T-cell activity have been proposed as potential mechanisms. Evidence suggests abnormal T-cell activity, including elevated levels of Th1 inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, INF-γ, IL-6, and IP-10 in blood samples from PFAPA patients. Increased production of IL-1β has also been observed, consistent with an abnormal innate immune response. Studies investigating potential genetic mutations associated with PFAPA have yielded inconclusive results. The cause of PFAPA is unknown. It is often discussed alongside other periodic fever syndromes, but it remains unclear whether its etiology is primarily genetic or triggered by an initial infection. PFAPA must be differentiated from other conditions such as cyclic neutropenia, familial Mediterranean fever (FMF), familial Hibernian fever (FHF), and hyperglobulinemia D syndrome. The incidence of PFAPA syndrome is approximately 23 per 100,000 children under the age of 5 worldwide. While the exact prevalence is unknown, it appears to be more common than other autoinflammatory disorders. PFAPA predominantly affects children aged 2 to 5 years, though adult-onset cases have been reported. There is no racial predilection, and the syndrome affects males and females equally. There are no established risk factors for PFAPA syndrome. Routine screening for PFAPA is not recommended due to insufficient evidence. Patients with PFAPA typically develop symptoms in early childhood, between the ages of 2 and 5. The syndrome manifests as periodic episodes of high fever lasting 3 to 6 days, accompanied by aphthous ulcers, non-infectious exudative pharyngitis, and cervical lymphadenopathy. These episodes usually recur every 21 to 28 days. Between episodes, and even during them, children appear healthy. Current research indicates that PFAPA does not lead to other diseases and resolves spontaneously as the child grows older, with no long-term effects. The diagnosis of PFAPA syndrome is made based on specific diagnostic criteria, which include the exclusion of possible infections, immunodeficiency, monogenic autoinflammatory disorders, and cyclic neutropenia. Key symptoms include periodic high fever, aphthous ulcers, pharyngitis, and/or adenitis. Less common symptoms may include abdominal pain, diarrhea, headache, skin rash, and arthralgia. Physical examination findings in PFAPA patients may reveal high fever, exudative pharyngitis, aphthous ulcers, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Laboratory findings during febrile episodes may include leukocytosis (with a predominance of neutrophils) and elevated inflammatory markers such as ESR and CRP. These markers are typically normal between episodes. Quantitative immunoglobulin levels are generally normal or near normal. At the onset of fever, inflammatory markers may also be normal. CD64 and CXCL10 have been proposed as potential specific biomarkers for PFAPA, but further studies are needed to confirm their association. There are no findings on ECG, X-ray, echocardiography, ultrasound, CT scan, MRI, or other imaging modalities associated with PFAPA syndrome. There is no definitive treatment for PFAPA syndrome, and management primarily involves supportive care. A single dose of prednisone (2 mg per kg body mass) at the onset of each fever episode has been shown to terminate the fever within several hours. However, in some children, prednisone may cause episodes to occur more frequently and regularly. Daily administration of colchicine has been associated with a decreased frequency of episodes. IL-1 blockade with drugs such as anakinra, rilonacept, and canakinumab has shown promising results, leading to a shortened disease course and, in some cases, complete resolution of symptoms. Adenotonsillectomy is recommended for patients who do not respond to medical treatment. However, recent studies suggest moderate-quality evidence supporting the role of surgery in managing these patients. A careful evaluation of risks and benefits is advised before proceeding with surgery. There are no established measures for the primary or secondary prevention of PFAPA syndrome.
